title: Making an RTS with little to know coding knowledge, tips?
author: AncientPaper2994
selftext:
Hi, 

I am developing an RTS (mix between ostfront and company of heroes) I have quite a functional game that looks already really good and functions properly with some depth.

I am a bit worried about security, especially for multiplayer, my plan was to launch it through steam but perhaps to hire a network coder to review the code. 

Still I am generally a bit worried because I don't really understand the code. I only understand the systems behind them. 

Anyone tips , anyone who went through this process?

comments.author: samcripp
comments.body:
Well I 100% recommend you learn to program. You don't have to be the greatest programmer in the planet, but understanding code is half the battle.

As far as security, that will likely be grouped into 2 to 3 groups. server side and client side, and if there is a third party involve, thats kinda of its own group as well, like if you are using firebase for auth or something like that.

Without the programing knowledge, definitely have someone look at your code, and review it. it never hurts to have a second pair of eyes look at it.

comments.author: ChadSexman
comments.body:
You could probably vibe this, but I recommend dropping the multiplayer part for this first game. Even with heavy AI use, you’re adding a ton of complexity to your project.

To elaborate: RTS typically have a high number of units. If implemented poorly, then you’re going to be sending a ton of data across the network. AI can optimize quite well, but you need to know what to ask for and what to look for while profiling.

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body: My tip is to pick a different genre. An RTS is a lot of work and AI only solves some problems.

comments.author: LastingDynamicsGames
comments.body:
For an RTS, "is the multiplayer secure" mostly comes down to three questions, and they make a good brief for the network coder.

What does a client send? Ideally only commands ("move these units here", "build X"), never positions, health or resources.

What gets checked when a command arrives? Do you own those units, can you afford it, is that ability off cooldown. Unchecked commands are where most cheats live.

Lockstep or server-authoritative? With lockstep every machine holds the full game state, so map hacks are possible; for a small launch that is usually an acceptable trade.

On Steam, use its networking with the relay so players never see each other's IPs, and Steam auth tickets instead of your own login. Before the review, ask your AI for a one-page list of every network message and what is validated on receipt. It makes the review faster and the gaps tend to show up on their own.
